title: ⚔️ Chapter boss ⭐⭐⭐: who did it, who is blamed, what the notice really says

questions.prompt: Nizar went to the bookshop with the money he had saved and came home with a dictionary that now stands on his own desk, for his own use. Which sentence reports that in correct English?

options.text: Nizar bought himself a new dictionary.
Nizar bought him a new dictionary.
Nizar bought his self a new dictionary.
Nizar bought to himself a new dictionary.

questions.explanation: "Nizar bought himself a new dictionary." is right: the person who pays and the person the book is for are one and the same, and the reflexive is what English puts in that place, straight after the verb. "Nizar bought him a new dictionary." is perfectly correct English, but it tells a different story: an object pronoun always points away from the subject, so the dictionary would be a present for somebody else. "Nizar bought his self a new dictionary." splits a word that English writes in one piece; there is himself, and there is no his self. And "Nizar bought to himself a new dictionary." adds a preposition the pattern refuses: you buy somebody something, or you buy something for somebody, so bought a dictionary for himself would have been another correct way of saying it, but never bought to himself.

questions.prompt: The results have just been posted and four pupils are talking in the corridor. All four sentences below are built on should have or shouldn't have plus a past participle. Which one expresses a regret about the speaker's own choice, and not a reproach aimed at somebody else?

options.text: You shouldn't have left the last page blank.
You should have asked the teacher for the reading list.
Hedi should have started his revision much earlier.
I should have checked my answers before the bell.

questions.explanation: "I should have checked my answers before the bell." is the regret: the form says that a sensible action was not carried out, and because the subject is the speaker, what comes out is regret and not blame. "You shouldn't have left the last page blank." uses the same structure, but the subject is the person spoken to, so the sentence blames that person for something already done, which is a reproach. "You should have asked the teacher for the reading list." is a reproach too, this time for an action that was never carried out at all. And "Hedi should have started his revision much earlier." moves the blame onto a third person who is named, which changes nothing to the value: the speaker is judging somebody else, not looking back on a paper of their own.

questions.prompt: A form teacher says four things to the same pupil in the course of one morning. One of them is a warning: it announces something unpleasant that will follow at once if the pupil does not act. Which sentence is the warning?

options.text: You ought to give a hand to the pupils who joined the class in January.
You had better hand in your file before the office closes.
You needn't copy out the whole text; the first paragraph is enough.
You should read a page of English every evening.

questions.explanation: "You had better hand in your file before the office closes." is the warning: had better always has a bad result standing behind it, and here the result is named by the sentence itself, since the office will shut and the file will not be in. "You ought to give a hand to the pupils who joined the class in January." states a duty, what a decent classmate does, and nothing unpleasant is announced if the pupil does nothing. "You needn't copy out the whole text; the first paragraph is enough." does the opposite of warning: it lifts an effort the pupil believed compulsory. And "You should read a page of English every evening." is ordinary advice about a habit, with no deadline over it and no consequence attached.

questions.prompt: Read this notice posted at the entrance of a secondary school in Bizerte before the end-of-term exams, then answer. "Mobile phones must not be brought into the exam rooms. Candidates are advised to arrive at least fifteen minutes before the paper begins. There is no need to bring squared paper: it is provided on every desk. Bags are to be left in the corridor." Which of these four statements is true according to the notice?

options.text: A candidate who arrives five minutes before the paper begins is breaking a rule.
A candidate who brings squared paper is breaking a rule.
A candidate who brings squared paper breaks no rule, but will not need it.
A candidate who leaves a bag in the corridor is breaking a rule.

questions.explanation: "A candidate who brings squared paper breaks no rule, but will not need it." is what the notice says: there is no need to means only that the action is unnecessary, and a sentence that releases you never forbids you. "A candidate who arrives five minutes before the paper begins is breaking a rule." reads are advised to as an order, when advice leaves the candidate free; arriving late is unwise, and it is still not against this notice. "A candidate who brings squared paper is breaking a rule." makes the same mistake the other way round, turning there is no need to into a ban, which only must not and are not allowed can do, as the first line does for phones. And "A candidate who leaves a bag in the corridor is breaking a rule." reverses the last line: leaving the bag there is exactly what the notice asks for.

questions.prompt: Read this paragraph, written by a pupil for the school magazine, then answer. "(1) A uniform is not the small, harmless thing our head teacher says it is. (2) It is true that it settles in advance a question that would otherwise come up every single morning. (3) But it takes away the one decision a pupil still makes alone before leaving home. (4) A school that wants us to think for ourselves cannot begin by dressing us all the same." Which sentence is the point the writer concedes to the other side?

options.text: Sentence 2, because it grants the other side a real advantage.
Sentence 1, because it opens by rejecting the head teacher's view.
Sentence 3, because it is introduced by the linker But.
Sentence 4, because it states what the whole paragraph is aiming at.

questions.explanation: "Sentence 2, because it grants the other side a real advantage." is right: a concession is the one sentence in which a writer admits that the people he is arguing against have a fair point, and It is true that is the expression English keeps for that move. "Sentence 1, because it opens by rejecting the head teacher's view." describes the thesis, the position the writer defends from the first line, which is the opposite of a concession. "Sentence 3, because it is introduced by the linker But." mistakes the answer for the admission: But marks the return to the writer's own argument, and it can only come after a concession. And "Sentence 4, because it states what the whole paragraph is aiming at." names the conclusion, which by definition follows the writer's side and never the other one.

questions.prompt: Rania has written this line on her vocabulary card: "to distinguish = to be exactly like the others". Her definition belongs to another verb of the theme. Which of these four gives the real meaning of the verb she wrote?

options.text: to follow a rule that the whole group follows
to see or to show the difference between two things
to put an end to something so that it no longer shows
to look at a piece of work again to make sure it is right

questions.explanation: "to see or to show the difference between two things" is the meaning of distinguish, and it works in both directions: you distinguish one twin from the other when you can tell them apart, and a badge distinguishes a school from its neighbours when it sets the two apart for everybody to see. "to follow a rule that the whole group follows" is the meaning of conform to, and it is in fact the meaning Rania wrote on her card, which is how the two verbs got exchanged: they are near opposites. "to put an end to something so that it no longer shows" defines suppress, the verb the uniform file uses of a school accused of hiding what makes each pupil different. And "to look at a piece of work again to make sure it is right" defines check, which belongs to the exam lesson and has nothing to do with telling two things apart.
